paraphrase: Some people do not know from which direction they have come, or whether their soul is one that is reborn. One who knows, by his own insight or from others, 'my soul is reborn; I came from this direction' — he believes in the soul, in the world, in karma and in action.
speaker: Mahāvīra (as reported by Sudharman to Jambū)
notes: The fourfold 'believer in the soul, world, karma and action' (āyāvāī, logāvāī, kammāvāī, kiriyāvāī); wording paraphrased.

paraphrase: The six lessons that follow describe the harm done to earth-bodied, water-bodied, fire-bodied, plant-bodied, mobile and wind-bodied beings by those who act for their own ends, and teach that one who understands this harm renounces causing it, having it caused, and approving it.
speaker: Mahāvīra (as reported by Sudharman to Jambū)
notes: The order of the six classes in Book I (earth, water, fire, plants, mobile beings, wind) differs from the later standard order; lesson-level refs.

paraphrase: All beings are fond of life, like pleasure, hate pain, shun destruction, like to live, long to live: to all, life is dear.
speaker: Mahāvīra (as reported by Sudharman to Jambū)
notes: Lesson-level ref (1.2.3); the Prakrit wording is well known but not quoted here.

paraphrase: Whoever gives up the idea of 'mine' gives up what is his; the sage who has seen the path is one for whom there is nothing that is 'mine'.
speaker: Mahāvīra (as reported by Sudharman to Jambū)
notes: Ref at lesson level; moderate confidence.

paraphrase: The unwise sleep; the sages are always awake. Know that in this world suffering comes from delusion, and, seeing the fear, be vigilant.
speaker: Mahāvīra (as reported by Sudharman to Jambū)

paraphrase: He who knows one knows all; he who knows all knows one. The one who sees (pāsaga) has no designation or condition (upādhi) left.
speaker: Mahāvīra (as reported by Sudharman to Jambū)

original.text: je egaṃ jāṇai se savvaṃ jāṇai, je savvaṃ jāṇai se egaṃ jāṇai
original.edition: from memory (skeleton); wording to be checked against a critical edition

notes: The second sentence is paraphrased from the end of the same lesson (moderate confidence on its placement).

paraphrase: All the Arhats and Bhagavats of the past, present and future say this: no living being, no creature, no soul, no being of any kind should be killed, ruled over, enslaved, tormented or driven away. This is the pure, unchanging, eternal law (dharma), proclaimed by those who know the world.
speaker: Mahāvīra (as reported by Sudharman to Jambū)

paraphrase: You are the very one whom you intend to kill; you are the one you intend to rule over, to torment, to enslave, to drive away. The upright one lives knowing this, and therefore neither kills nor causes killing.
speaker: Mahāvīra (as reported by Sudharman to Jambū)
notes: Moderate confidence on the lesson number (1.5.5).

paraphrase: The liberated one cannot be described: all sounds recoil from it, reasoning does not reach it, the mind cannot grasp it. It is not long or short, round or square, black or white, fragrant or foul, bitter or sweet, heavy or light, cold or hot; it has no body, is not reborn, has no attachment; it is not female, male or neuter. It perceives, it knows; there is no analogy for it; its being is formless; there is no condition of the unconditioned, no word for it.
speaker: Mahāvīra (as reported by Sudharman to Jambū)
notes: Lesson-level ref; a composite paraphrase of the famous apophatic passage.

paraphrase: The lessons of the 'Liberation' (Vimokṣa) lecture describe monks who keep three robes and a bowl, two robes, one robe, or who go without clothes (acela) — each is told not to think of more garments when the cold season passes and to regard lightness (lāghava) as austerity; the naked monk bears the hardships of cold, heat and insects.
speaker: Mahāvīra (as reported by Sudharman to Jambū)
notes: Lesson assignment (three robes 1.8.4, two 1.8.5, one 1.8.6, none 1.8.7) from memory; moderate confidence. A canonical basis cited by both sides in the nudity debate.

paraphrase: The lecture closes by describing the kinds of death of a wise monk who, when the body can no longer support restraint, renounces food with full awareness — undertaken only at the proper time, without desire for life or for death, and never from despair (restricted theme: the text's conditions only, no procedure).
speaker: Mahāvīra (as reported by Sudharman to Jambū)
notes: Restricted: summary only. Ref approximate (the three forms — bhakta-pratyākhyāna, iṅgita-maraṇa, pādapopagamana — are treated in the last lessons of 1.8).

paraphrase: The 'Pillow of Righteousness' (Upadhānaśruta) describes how the Venerable Ascetic wandered: he wore the one robe for thirteen months and thereafter went naked; he meditated with eyes fixed, silent, avoiding company; in the pathless land of Lāḍha he was beaten and set upon by dogs and bore it; he took no medicine, fasted for long periods, and, free from sinfulness, meditated in the posture of kāyotsarga, not seeking comfort.
speaker: Sudharman (narrating)
notes: Lecture-level ref (four lessons).

paraphrase: The 'Bhāvanā' chapter tells Mahāvīra's life — his descent, the transfer of the embryo from Devānandā to Triśalā, his birth, his parents' devotion to Pārśva's teaching, his renunciation and omniscience — and then sets out the five great vows, each with five supporting reflections (bhāvanā), twenty-five in all.
speaker: Mahāvīra (as reported by Sudharman to Jambū)
notes: Chapter-level ref (Book II, cūlā 3).

paraphrase: One should understand and break the bond. What did the hero (Mahāvīra) call the bond, and by knowing what does one break it? One who owns possessions, living or lifeless, or consents to others owning them, or who kills or has others kill, is not freed from suffering.
speaker: Mahāvīra (as reported by Sudharman to Jambū)
notes: The opening verses of the Sūtrakṛtāṅga ('bujjhijja tiuṭṭijjā…').

paraphrase: It states and rejects rival views: that only the five elements exist and the self perishes with them; that there is one self appearing in many forms, as one earth appears as many things; that soul and body are one; that the self is inactive; that the self is a sixth, eternal element; and that there are only momentary aggregates (the Buddhist view). Those who hold them are not free from suffering.
speaker: Mahāvīra (as reported by Sudharman to Jambū)
notes: The opponents' positions are reported by the Jain text (reported_by_opponent). Lesson-level ref; Śīlāṅka identifies the views (Cārvāka, Vedānta-like ekātmavāda, Sāṃkhya, Buddhism).

paraphrase: The fatalists say that pleasure and pain are neither caused by oneself nor by another but are determined by destiny (niyati); the text answers that such teachers, not understanding what is and is not caused by oneself, wander in saṃsāra.
speaker: Mahāvīra (as reported by Sudharman to Jambū)
notes: Niyativāda (the Ājīvika position) as reported by the Jain text.

paraphrase: This is the essence of wisdom: not to kill anything. Know that non-harm and equality (samaya) — just this much is the teaching.
speaker: Mahāvīra (as reported by Sudharman to Jambū)
notes: The verse recurs at 1.11.10; verse-number moderate confidence.

paraphrase: Wake up! Why do you not wake up? Enlightenment is hard to gain in the next world; the nights that pass do not return, and human life is not easily obtained again.
speaker: Ṛṣabha to his sons (per the commentary)
notes: The commentators set this 'Vaitālīya' lecture in Ṛṣabha's mouth addressing his sons; moderate confidence on that framing.

paraphrase: The lecture on women (Strīparijñā) warns the monk of the ways in which women tempt and bind a renouncer and describes the servitude of the monk who falls; it counsels avoiding intimacy and solitude with them.
speaker: Mahāvīra (as reported by Sudharman to Jambū)
notes: Recorded as the text states it (addressed to male monks); lecture-level ref.

paraphrase: The praise of Mahāvīra (Vīrastuti): asked by monks, brāhmaṇas and householders, Sudharman describes the Jñātṛ son as the all-knowing, the best of those who have conquered, like Mount Meru among mountains, the ocean among waters, and the one who taught the dharma after knowing it himself.
speaker: Sudharman
notes: Lecture-level ref ('pucchissu ṇaṃ samaṇā māhaṇā ya…').

paraphrase: The 'Assembly' (Samavasaraṇa) lecture groups all other teachers under four doctrines — those who teach that action bears fruit (kriyāvāda), that it does not (akriyāvāda), that knowledge is useless (ajñānavāda), and that discipline or reverence alone saves (vinayavāda) — and says that the Jina, knowing the world and its beings, teaches beyond their partial views.
speaker: Mahāvīra (as reported by Sudharman to Jambū)
notes: Later tradition (the niryukti) counts 363 views: 180 kriyāvāda, 84 akriyāvāda, 67 ajñānavāda, 32 vinayavāda.

paraphrase: The parable of the lotus (Puṇḍarīka): a great white lotus stands in the middle of a pond; four men from the four directions wade in to pluck it and sink in the mud; a monk standing on the bank calls, 'Rise, O lotus!' and it comes. The pond is the world, the mud desires, the four men the teachers of the soul-is-body view, of the five elements, of a creator-self and of fate; the monk is the one who teaches the true dharma; the lotus is the king (the person to be freed).
speaker: Mahāvīra (as reported by Sudharman to Jambū)
notes: Chapter-level ref.

paraphrase: Ārdraka, on his way to Mahāvīra, answers in turn Gośāla (who charges Mahāvīra with inconsistency for once living alone and now teaching crowds), Buddhist monks (who say intention alone matters, so that roasting a child mistaken for a gourd would bring no sin), brāhmaṇas (who praise feeding two thousand snātakas), Vedāntin ascetics, and hermits who kill one elephant a year to live without harming many small beings; he refutes each by the standard of non-harm and right knowledge.
speaker: Ārdraka
notes: The opponents' positions are reported by the Jain text.

paraphrase: At Nālandā, Udaka Peḍhālaputta, a monk of Pārśva's line, questions Gautama on whether the layman's limited vow of non-harm is sound when beings change their state; Gautama answers, and Udaka accepts Mahāvīra's fivefold discipline.
speaker: Gautama and Udaka

paraphrase: Among its tens, the Sthānāṅga lists ten 'wonders' (accheraga) of this descending age — events that should not happen but did: among them a woman becoming a Tīrthaṅkara (Mallī), the removal of Mahāvīra's embryo to another womb, an attack on a Jina (Gośāla's), Mahāvīra's first assembly in which no one took vows, and the worship of the unrestrained.
notes: The full list of ten is given in cpt:ten-accheras (moderate confidence); section-level ref.

paraphrase: Among its sevens, the Sthānāṅga names the seven schismatics (nihnava) of Mahāvīra's teaching — Jamāli, Tiṣyagupta, Āṣāḍha, Aśvamitra, Gaṅga, Rohagupta (Ṣaḍulūka) and Goṣṭhāmāhila — each of whom denied one point of doctrine.
notes: Section-level ref.

paraphrase: The thirty-four supernatural excellences (atiśaya) of the Buddhas (Jinas): among them hair and nails that do not grow, a body free of disease and sweat, breath fragrant as a lotus, invisible eating and evacuation, a wheel of dharma moving before them, a voice in Ardhamāgadhī understood by all beings in their own speech, and the absence of plague and famine around them.
notes: Sample items only; that eating is 'not seen' is a Śvetāmbara atiśaya, while Digambaras deny eating altogether.

paraphrase: The Samavāyāṅga's appendix describes the twelve-limbed scripture limb by limb, including the Dṛṣṭivāda with its five parts and fourteen Pūrvas, and lists the illustrious persons of the age.
notes: Section-level ref (the 'duvālasaṅga' description at the end of the text).

paraphrase: The Bhagavatī opens with the fivefold salutation — to the Arhats, the Siddhas, the Ācāryas, the Upādhyāyas and all the Sādhus in the world — and adds a salutation to the Brāhmī script and to the scripture.

original.text: namo arihaṃtāṇaṃ / namo siddhāṇaṃ / namo āyariyāṇaṃ / namo uvajjhāyāṇaṃ / namo loe savvasāhūṇaṃ
original.edition: from memory (skeleton); wording to be checked against a critical edition

notes: Opening maṅgala of the text; the salutation to the Brāhmī script ('namo baṃbhīe livīe') is recalled with moderate confidence.

paraphrase: Gautama's first questions: is what is moving already moved, what is being produced already produced, what is being bound already bound, what is dying already dead? Mahāvīra answers yes — the action in progress is, in a respect, already accomplished.
speaker: Mahāvīra and Gautama
notes: 'calamāṇe calie…'; this doctrine is what Jamāli later rejected. Moderate confidence on the exact list of pairs.

paraphrase: Kālāsaveśiputra, a monk of Pārśva's line, asks Mahāvīra's elders what equanimity (sāmāyika) and its purpose are; they answer: the self is sāmāyika, and the self is the purpose of sāmāyika. Convinced, he accepts the fivefold discipline.
speaker: the elders (sthaviras)
notes: 'āyā ṇe ajjo sāmāie, āyā ṇe ajjo sāmāiyassa aṭṭhe' — wording recalled with moderate confidence.

paraphrase: Skandaka's questions: Is the world finite or infinite? Mahāvīra answers by four respects — as substance the world is one and finite; in space it is finite; in time it is without end, having always been and always to be; in its modes (colours, forms and the rest) it is infinite. He answers likewise of the soul, of liberation (siddhi) and of the liberated one.
speaker: Mahāvīra
notes: The fourfold analysis by substance, place, time and state (dravya, kṣetra, kāla, bhāva).

paraphrase: Are souls eternal or not eternal? In one respect eternal, in another not: as substance (dravya) they are eternal; as modes (paryāya — their states and births) they are not eternal.
speaker: Mahāvīra
notes: The doctrine is certain; the location (7.2 or nearby) is low confidence.

paraphrase: Jamāli, Mahāvīra's nephew and son-in-law, falling ill asked his monks to spread a bed; hearing 'it is being spread' and then finding it not yet spread, he concluded that what is being done is not done, against Mahāvīra's teaching that what is being done is done. He would not accept correction and left with his followers; Priyadarśanā followed him, then returned.

The laywoman Jayantī asks: is it better to sleep or to be awake? For the unrighteous sleep is better, for then they harm no one; for the righteous wakefulness is better. Is strength or weakness better? Likewise. Will all beings capable of liberation (bhavya) be liberated, and will the world then be empty of them? No — as the rows of the sky's points are endless, so the capable are never exhausted.
speaker: Mahāvīra
notes: Moderate confidence on the exact analogy for the inexhaustibility of bhavyas.

paraphrase: The self is of eight kinds: as substance, as passion, as activity, as cognition (upayoga), as knowledge, as perception, as conduct and as energy; and a thing may be said to be self, not-self, or inexpressible, according to the respect in which it is considered.
notes: An early form of conditional predication; section ref low confidence.

paraphrase: The history of Gośāla Maṅkhaliputra: how he attached himself to Mahāvīra for six years, learned from him the power of fiery energy (tejoleśyā), separated from him, taught that all is determined by fate, and at Śrāvastī attacked Mahāvīra and burned two of his monks with that power; the fire turned back on Gośāla, who before dying confessed that he was not a Jina. Mahāvīra suffered a burning illness for six months and was restored with food prepared by the laywoman Revatī.
notes: Gośāla's teaching is reported here by his opponents (reported_by_opponent). The nature of Revatī's preparation is itself a matter of interpretation; Śvetāmbaras cite the episode as showing the omniscient takes food and medicine.

paraphrase: Prince Megha, newly a monk, lay awake jostled by monks passing his bed and resolved to return home; Mahāvīra reminded him that in a past life, as an elephant, he held up one foot for days during a forest fire so as not to crush a hare that had taken shelter beneath it, and by that compassion gained human birth. Megha was steadied and became a great ascetic.
speaker: Mahāvīra

paraphrase: A merchant gives five rice grains each to his four daughters-in-law and later asks for them back: one threw them away, one ate them, one kept them safe, and one had them sown and returned cartloads. So monks who receive the five great vows may lose, consume, guard or increase them.
notes: The Rohiṇī parable.

paraphrase: Mallī, daughter of King Kumbha of Mithilā, was the nineteenth Tīrthaṅkara. Courted by six kings, her companions in a former life, she had a hollow golden image of herself made and daily put a morsel of food inside; when the kings came she opened it and the stench overwhelmed them; she taught them that the body is such, and all renounced. She had been born a woman because in her past life as King Mahābala she practised more fasting than her companions by deceit.
notes: Śvetāmbara canonical account; the Digambaras reject both the text and a female Tīrthaṅkara.

paraphrase: In the story of Draupadī, before her svayaṃvara she bathes and worships the images of the Jinas (jiṇa-paḍimā) in the palace shrine.
notes: A passage cited by Mūrtipūjakas for image worship; Sthānakavāsīs read it differently (e.g. as worship before Draupadī became a Jain laywoman, or dispute the reading). Moderate confidence on details.

paraphrase: Two tortoises foraging near a pond are spied by two jackals; the one that put out its limbs was killed, the one that kept its limbs withdrawn in its shell survived. So the monk who guards his senses is safe; the one who lets them out perishes.

Ānanda, a wealthy householder of Vāṇijagrāma, takes before Mahāvīra the five small vows and seven supplementary vows, limiting his wealth, fields, cattle and trade; later he performs the eleven lay stages (pratimā), gains clairvoyance and dies a peaceful death. When Gautama doubted him, Mahāvīra told Gautama that he, not the layman, must ask forgiveness.

Saddālaputra, a potter and follower of Gośāla, believed that all happens by fate without effort. Mahāvīra asked him: if a man stole or smashed your pots or assaulted your wife, would you punish him? He said yes — then, said Mahāvīra, you do not really hold that there is no effort or exertion. Saddālaputra became Mahāvīra's lay disciple.
speaker: Mahāvīra

paraphrase: Gajasukumāla, Kṛṣṇa's young brother, became a monk under Ariṣṭanemi and stood in meditation in a cremation ground; the brāhmaṇa Somila, his would-be father-in-law, set a rim of clay on his head and filled it with burning coals. Without anger, regarding Somila as a helper in shedding karma, he attained omniscience and liberation that very night.
notes: Chapter ref (varga 3, ch. 8) moderate-low confidence.

paraphrase: Arjuna the gardener, possessed by a yakṣa, killed many people in Rājagṛha; stopped by the layman Sudarśana's fearless faith, he became a monk of Mahāvīra, bore the beatings and curses of the townspeople with equanimity for six months, and attained liberation.
notes: Chapter ref low confidence.

paraphrase: Dhanya, a rich young man, became a monk and fasted with such rigour that his body is described limb by limb as withered like dry leaves and pods; Mahāvīra praised him to King Śreṇika as the greatest ascetic among his monks. He was reborn in the highest heaven.
notes: Restricted theme (prolonged fasting): the text's description only; no practice instruction.

paraphrase: Non-harm (ahiṃsā) is praised under sixty names: it is the island for those in the sea, the refuge, the support, the mother of all beings, the rest and nourishment of the world; it is what the Tīrthaṅkaras teach and the protector of all beings, moving and unmoving.
notes: First saṃvara-dvāra; the count of sixty names and sample epithets from memory.

paraphrase: The first door of inflow is violence (hiṃsā), described by its names, its forms, those who commit it and the terrible fruit it bears in hell and animal births; the other four doors are falsehood, theft, unchastity and possessiveness.

Mṛgāputra is born blind, deaf, without limbs, a mere lump of flesh kept in a cellar, because in a former life as a cruel governor he oppressed his subjects; the stories of the first book show how evil deeds ripen as suffering, those of the second how good deeds ripen as happiness.

The text ends with the liberated (siddha): where they are obstructed, where they are established, where they leave the body and where they reach perfection — beyond the summit of the world, on the Īṣatprāgbhārā earth; bodiless, dense with soul-units, endowed with knowledge and perception, they enjoy an unobstructed happiness that no god possesses.
notes: Section-level ref (final section).

paraphrase: King Paesi, who held that soul and body are one, tells Keśin of his experiments: he sealed a thief alive in an iron jar and found no hole by which a soul left; weighed a man before and after death and found no difference; cut a body to pieces and found no soul. Keśin answers with similes — sound escapes a sealed chamber without a hole; a leather bag weighs the same filled with air or empty; fire is not found by chopping the fire-drill wood — and Paesi accepts the teaching.
speaker: Keśin
notes: The materialist experiments are reported by the Jain text (the king is an opponent who converts). Similes recalled with moderate confidence on their pairing.

paraphrase: The god Sūryābha comes from his celestial palace to honour Mahāvīra and stages a divine dance; the text describes his palace, in which he worships the images of the Jinas with water, sandal, flowers, incense and lamps.
notes: The Mūrtipūjakas' prime canonical example of image worship; Sthānakavāsīs read it as the conduct of gods, not an injunction for humans.

paraphrase: The liberated are of fifteen kinds: liberated as Tīrthaṅkaras or not; in the time of a Tīrthaṅkara's congregation or outside it; self-enlightened, enlightened by an external cause (pratyekabuddha), or taught by the enlightened; in the female, male or neuter sex; in the Jain monk's garb, in other garb, or as householders; singly or several at once.
notes: The same list appears in the Nandī; Śvetāmbaras cite 'strīliṅga-siddha' and 'gṛhiliṅga-siddha' against the Digambara positions.

paraphrase: Describes the six ages of the descending half-cycle and the life of Ṛṣabha, first king and first Tīrthaṅkara, who in the transition from the age of wish-fulfilling trees taught people the seventy-two arts for men and sixty-four for women, and cooking, pottery and the other crafts, then renounced and founded the dharma.
notes: Chapter-level ref (vakṣaskāra 2), moderate confidence.

paraphrase: The first lecture, on discipline (vinaya): the good pupil obeys the teacher's commands, stays near him, understands his gestures and hints; the undisciplined pupil is like a bad bullock, like a rotten-eared bitch driven from everywhere; the teacher is pleased with the disciplined and imparts learning to him.
speaker: Mahāvīra (tradition)

paraphrase: The twenty-two hardships (parīṣaha) that a monk must bear without swerving from the path, for the sake of shedding karma: hunger, thirst, cold, heat, insect bites, nakedness (acela), discontent, women, wandering, the place of sitting, lodging, abuse, beating, begging, not receiving, illness, the touch of grass, dirt, honour and reverence, intellect, ignorance and lack of faith.
notes: The Uttarādhyayana treats 'acela' as bearing either nakedness or poor clothing — a point read differently by the sects.

paraphrase: Four supreme things are hard for a living being to obtain: human birth, hearing the dharma, faith in it, and energy in self-restraint.

original.text: cattāri paramaṃgāṇi dullahāṇīha jaṃtuṇo / māṇusattaṃ suī saddhā saṃjamammi ya vīriyaṃ
original.edition: from memory (skeleton); wording to be checked against a critical edition

paraphrase: Life cannot be mended once broken; therefore be not careless. For one who has reached old age there is no protection; think how the careless, violent and unrestrained will fare.
notes: 'asaṃkhayaṃ jīviya mā pamāyae'.

paraphrase: There are two ways of dying: the death against one's will (akāma-maraṇa) of the ignorant, who cling to pleasures and die in fear, and the death with one's will (sakāma-maraṇa) of the wise and restrained, who die calm and are reborn among the gods or reach liberation. The wise one, when death comes, should give up the body with composure.
When Indra, disguised as a brāhmaṇa, told the renouncing king Nami that his city Mithilā was burning, Nami answered: 'Happy we live, we who own nothing; when Mithilā burns, nothing of mine burns.'
speaker: Nami
notes: Nami is a pratyekabuddha; verse number moderate confidence.

paraphrase: Though a man should conquer thousands upon thousands of valiant foes in battle, greater is his victory if he conquers only himself. Fight with yourself; why fight external foes? He who conquers himself by himself wins happiness; difficult to conquer are the five senses, anger, pride, deceit and greed — and the self.
speaker: Nami
notes: 9.34–36 (moderate confidence on numbers); the name 'Jina' ('conqueror') is glossed by this teaching.

paraphrase: As a withered leaf falls from the tree when its days are over, so the life of men comes to its end: Gautama, be not careless for a moment. Life is short like a dewdrop on the tip of a blade of grass; human birth is rare; the body decays — Gautama, be not careless for a moment.
speaker: Mahāvīra

original.edition: from memory (skeleton); wording to be checked against a critical edition

notes: The refrain ends every verse of the lecture; only the refrain is quoted.

paraphrase: The outcaste (Śvapāka) monk Harikeśa, mocked at a brāhmaṇa sacrifice, is defended by a yakṣa; he teaches that birth is nothing and virtue everything, and describes the true sacrifice: austerity is the fire, the soul the fire-place, right exertion the ladle, the body the fuel of dung, karma the fuel burned, restraint the peace-formula — this is the offering praised by the seers.
speaker: Harikeśa
notes: The fire image is at 12.44 (moderate confidence); chapter ref given.

paraphrase: The self is the doer and the undoer of its own suffering and happiness; the self well established is its own friend, the self badly established its own enemy.
speaker: the monk Anāthin
notes: From the dialogue in which the monk explains that he was 'unprotected' (anātha) until he renounced; verse number moderate confidence.

paraphrase: Ariṣṭanemi, riding to his wedding with Rājīmatī, heard the cries of animals penned for the feast, had them freed, and renounced; Rājīmatī also renounced, and when his brother Rathanemi, now a monk, desired her in a cave, she rebuked him — better to die than to return to what one has vomited — and he returned to his vows.

At Śrāvastī, Keśin of Pārśva's line and Gautama of Mahāvīra's meet and ask why Pārśva taught a fourfold law and allowed an under- and upper garment while Vardhamāna taught a fivefold law and nakedness. Gautama answers that the first Jina's disciples were simple and slow, the last Jina's crooked and slow, and those between simple and wise; so the law was stated in the way each could keep it; outward marks exist for recognition in the world, but the true means to liberation are knowledge, faith and conduct. Keśin then questions him in figures — the enemy, the fetters, the creeper, the fire, the unruly horse, the boat, the light, the safe place — and, satisfied, accepts the fivefold law.
speaker: Gautama

paraphrase: The eight 'mothers of the doctrine' (pravacana-mātā): five carefulnesses (samiti) — in walking, speaking, seeking alms, handling things, and disposing of excreta — and three guards (gupti) — of mind, speech and body. All the teaching is contained in them.

The true brāhmaṇa: not by shaving is one a śramaṇa, nor by the syllable Oṃ a brāhmaṇa, nor by living in the forest a sage, nor by a bark garment an ascetic; by equanimity one is a śramaṇa, by chastity a brāhmaṇa, by knowledge a sage, by austerity an ascetic. By one's acts one becomes a brāhmaṇa, a kṣatriya, a vaiśya or a śūdra; him we call a brāhmaṇa who is free from attachment and harms no being.
speaker: the monk Jayaghoṣa
notes: Chapter-level ref (the key verses are c. 25.29–33); parallels the Brāhmaṇavagga of the Dhammapada.

paraphrase: The rules of monastic routine (sāmācārī): the ten points of correct conduct toward teacher and fellow monks, and the division of the day and night into quarters — in the day, study in the first, meditation in the second, alms in the third, study again in the fourth; at night, study, meditation, sleep and study.

The path to liberation (mokkhamaggagaī) consists of knowledge, faith, conduct and austerity. Knowledge is of five kinds; the substances are six (the media of motion and rest, space, time, matter and souls); the real categories are nine (soul, non-soul, bondage, merit, demerit, inflow, stopping, shedding, liberation); faith is belief in these as they truly are. By knowledge one knows things, by faith one believes, by conduct one restrains, by austerity one is purified.
notes: Chapter-level; the fourfold path (with tapas) is the Uttarādhyayana's formulation, the Tattvārthasūtra's threefold path (1.1) absorbs austerity into conduct.

paraphrase: Without right faith there is no right knowledge; without knowledge no virtuous conduct; without virtues no liberation; without liberation no nirvāṇa.
notes: Verse number moderate confidence.

paraphrase: Seventy-three questions on the fruits of practices: e.g. what does one gain by equanimity? — cessation of sinful activity; by praising the twenty-four Jinas? — purity of faith; by repentance? — the closing of the holes in one's vows; by study? — the destruction of knowledge-obscuring karma; by forgiveness? — joy of mind.
notes: Sample answers paraphrased from memory.

paraphrase: Austerity is of two kinds: external — fasting, eating less than one's fill, limiting the kinds of alms accepted, giving up tasty food, bodily endurance, and seclusion; internal — atonement, humility, service, study, meditation and abandonment of the body. As a lake whose inflow is stopped dries up, so the karma of the restrained is burned away by austerity.
Attachment and aversion are the seeds of karma; karma arises from delusion, they say; karma is the root of birth and death, and birth and death they call suffering.
notes: Verse number moderate confidence.

paraphrase: The eight kinds of karma: knowledge-obscuring, perception-obscuring, feeling-producing, deluding, life-span, name (body-making), status (gotra) and obstructing; with their subdivisions, their durations and the amounts of karmic matter bound.

The six soul-colours (leśyā) — black, blue, grey (pigeon-coloured), fiery red, yellow (lotus-pink) and white — with their tastes, smells, touches and the dispositions they mark; the first three lead to bad births, the last three to good ones.

The analysis of the living and the non-living ends with the liberated: they stop where the medium of motion ends, at the summit of the world; they are liberated from the female, male and neuter sex, from the Jain monk's garb, from other garb and from the householder's state. The last verse says that the Enlightened Jñātaputra, having revealed these thirty-six lectures, attained nirvāṇa.
notes: The verses on female, male and neuter siddhas are around 36.49–50 (low confidence on numbering).

paraphrase: Dharma is the highest auspiciousness: non-harm, self-restraint and austerity. Even the gods bow to one whose mind is always set on dharma.

original.text: dhammo maṃgalamukkiṭṭhaṃ ahiṃsā saṃjamo tavo / devā vi taṃ namaṃsaṃti jassa dhamme sayā maṇo
original.edition: from memory (skeleton); wording to be checked against a critical edition

paraphrase: As the bee drinks from the flowers of a tree without harming the flowers and satisfies itself, so the monks, freed from attachments in this world, seek pure food given freely, like bees among flowers.

The six classes of living beings (earth, water, fire, wind, plants, mobile beings) are described, and the monk takes the five great vows and the sixth, not eating at night, renouncing harm to them in thought, word and deed, doing, causing and approving, for life.
notes: The chapter whose study qualifies a novice for 'great initiation' (chedopasthāpanā).

paraphrase: First knowledge, then compassion: so do all the restrained abide. What will the ignorant do? How will he know what is good and what is evil?
notes: 'paḍhamaṃ nāṇaṃ tao dayā'; verse number moderate confidence.

paraphrase: The clothes, bowl, blanket and broom that monks keep and use for the sake of restraint and modesty are not possessions: the Jñātaputra, the protector, did not call them possessiveness; possessiveness is attachment (mūrcchā) — so said the great seer.
notes: Verse numbers low-moderate confidence; the Śvetāmbara locus classicus, parallel to Tattvārthasūtra 7.17 'mūrcchā parigrahaḥ'.

paraphrase: Anger, pride, deceit and greed increase evil; one who desires his own good should vomit out these four faults. Anger destroys affection, pride destroys humility, deceit destroys friendship, greed destroys everything. Conquer anger by calm, pride by gentleness, deceit by straightforwardness, greed by contentment.
notes: Verse numbers moderate confidence (some editions 8.37–39).

paraphrase: The true monk (sa bhikkhū): one who, having left home at the Jina's word, harms no being, keeps his vows, begs pure food, is not angered by abuse, does not cling to his body, and is free from the pride of birth, of beauty, of gain and of learning.

The vow of equanimity: 'Venerable one, I undertake sāmāyika; I renounce all sinful activity for life (or for the set time), in three ways and by three means — I will not do it, nor cause it, nor approve it, in mind, speech or body; I repent of it, I censure it, I abandon that self (which committed it).'
notes: 'karemi bhante sāmāiyaṃ…' — paraphrased; the householder takes it for a set period, the monk for life.

paraphrase: The praise of the twenty-four Jinas (Logassa): 'I praise the Arhats who give light to the world, the makers of the ford of dharma, the conquerors — the twenty-four omniscient ones', naming Ṛṣabha and Ajita through Pārśva and Vardhamāna, and asking of them health, enlightenment and the highest concentration.
notes: The Jinas are asked for nothing worldly; tradition explains that they do not grant favours but are the pure object of praise.

paraphrase: In confession (pratikramaṇa) the practitioner turns back from transgressions — 'may my wrongdoing be fruitless' (micchā mi dukkaḍaṃ) — and asks and grants forgiveness to all beings: 'I forgive all living beings; may all beings forgive me; I have friendship with all beings and enmity with none.'
notes: The forgiveness verse ('khāmemi savvajīve…') is recited in pratikramaṇa; its exact canonical location (Āvaśyaka proper vs the later lay pratikramaṇa-sūtra) is uncertain — low confidence on the ref.

paraphrase: Four things are auspicious, four are highest in the world, in four I take refuge: the Arhats, the Siddhas, the Sādhus and the dharma taught by the omniscient. Taking these refuges, one confesses one's wrongs and rejoices in the good done by others.
notes: The 'cattāri maṅgalaṃ' formula also stands in the daily liturgy; whole-text ref.

paraphrase: Knowledge is of five kinds: sensory-mental (mati), scriptural (śruta), clairvoyant (avadhi), mind-reading (manaḥparyaya) and omniscient (kevala). The last three, gained by the soul directly, are 'direct' (pratyakṣa); the first two, gained through the senses and mind, are 'indirect' (parokṣa), though sensory knowledge may be called direct in the conventional sense.
notes: Section-level ref; the concession that sense-knowledge is 'conventionally direct' is systematized by Jinabhadra.

paraphrase: This twelve-limbed basket of the gaṇin never was not, never is not, never will not be; it was, is and will be — fixed, permanent, eternal, imperishable, unchanging, established, everlasting.
notes: Said of the dvādaśāṅga in its meaning (artha), which every Tīrthaṅkara re-proclaims; section-level ref (also in the Samavāyāṅga).

paraphrase: The Mahābhārata, the Rāmāyaṇa, the Vedas, Kauṭilya's treatise, the Buddhist and other scriptures are 'wrong scripture' (mithyā-śruta) for one of wrong view, but 'right scripture' for one of right view, since he uses them rightly; likewise the twelve Aṅgas are right scripture for the right-viewed and wrong scripture for the wrong-viewed.
notes: Sample list of titles from memory; the principle is the point.

paraphrase: Any word is to be understood by fourfold placement (nikṣepa): as a name (nāma), as a representation (sthāpanā) — in wood, painting, clay or the like, whether resembling the thing or not — as the substance without the actual state (dravya), and as the actual state (bhāva); 'āvaśyaka' is analysed in these four ways.
notes: Mūrtipūjakas cite sthāpanā-nikṣepa as canonical recognition of images as the Jina 'placed'; Sthānakavāsīs answer that it is a semantic category, not a command to worship.

paraphrase: The Venerable Ascetic Mahāvīra descended from the Puṣpottara heavenly palace into the womb of the brāhmaṇī Devānandā at Brāhmaṇakuṇḍagrāma, who saw fourteen great dreams — an elephant, a bull, a lion, the anointing of Śrī, a garland, the moon, the sun, a banner, a full vase, a lotus lake, the ocean, a celestial palace, a heap of jewels and a smokeless fire. Śakra, reflecting that Arhats are never born in low, poor, beggarly or brāhmaṇa families but in noble kṣatriya clans, sent Hariṇaigameṣin to transfer the embryo to the womb of the kṣatriyāṇī Triśalā, who then saw the same fourteen dreams.
notes: Section-level ref; the list order of the dreams follows the usual Śvetāmbara list (Digambaras count sixteen).

paraphrase: Mahāvīra lived thirty years as a householder, then renounced; for twelve years and more he neglected his body, bore all hardships from gods, men and animals with equanimity, and lived homeless, possessionless, watchful in the five carefulnesses and three guards. In the thirteenth year, under a śāla tree near Jṛmbhikagrāma on the bank of the Ṛjupālikā, squatting in the sun after a fast without water, in pure meditation, he attained the infinite, supreme, unobstructed, complete and full knowledge and perception called kevala.

At Pāvā, in the palace of King Hastipāla's scribes, in his seventy-second year, Mahāvīra passed away, freed from all suffering. On that night the eighteen confederate kings of Kāśī and Kośala, saying 'since the light of intelligence is gone, let us make an illumination of material matter', lit lamps; on that night Indrabhūti Gautama cut the bond of affection for his teacher and attained omniscience. The community he left numbered 14,000 monks under Indrabhūti and 36,000 nuns under Candanā, with 159,000 laymen and 318,000 laywomen.
notes: Numbers of the community recalled with moderate confidence.

paraphrase: The life of Pārśva, the Arhat 'beloved of men': born at Vārāṇasī to Aśvasena and Vāmā, he renounced at thirty, attained omniscience after eighty-four days, taught for about seventy years and reached nirvāṇa on Mount Sammeta aged a hundred; his community had 16,000 monks and 38,000 nuns (under Puṣpacūlā).
notes: Numbers recalled with moderate-low confidence.

paraphrase: The life of Ṛṣabha, 'the first king, the first mendicant, the first Jina, the first Tīrthaṅkara': born at the end of the third age, he taught the seventy-two arts, the sixty-four accomplishments of women and the hundred crafts, then renounced, and after omniscience taught for a vast period before nirvāṇa on Aṣṭāpada.

The list of elders: from Mahāvīra's eleven gaṇadharas through Sudharman, Jambū, Prabhava, Śayyambhava, Yaśobhadra, Sambhūtavijaya and Bhadrabāhu, Sthūlabhadra, Mahāgiri and Suhastin, with the schools (gaṇa), branches (śākhā) and families (kula) that issued from them, down to Devarddhigaṇi.
notes: Several gaṇas and kulas named here appear in the Kuṣāṇa-period inscriptions of Mathurā.

paraphrase: The rules of the rainy-season stay: a month and twenty nights after the rains begin the monks settle for the season and do not wander; they observe rules on alms, lodging and conduct; at Paryuṣaṇā they must forgive and ask forgiveness of one another — one who is reconciled is a 'fulfiller' (ārādhaka), one who is not is not, for the essence of monkhood is calm (uvasamasāraṃ khu sāmaṇṇaṃ).
notes: Section-level ref.

paraphrase: There are five grounds of judgment (vyavahāra) for monastic cases, to be used in order of availability: direct supernormal knowledge (āgama), scripture (śruta), instruction received (ājñā), retained tradition (dhāraṇā) and established practice (jīta). The same section fixes which texts a monk may be taught after how many years of monastic life.
notes: Section-level ref; the curriculum by years is recalled with low confidence.

paraphrase: It is not allowed for a nun to be without clothing (acela); nor for a nun to stay alone, or to practise certain exposed postures outside the dwelling.
notes: Uddeśaka reference low confidence; the rule that nuns may not go naked is the key point for the gender debate.

paraphrase: The eleven stages (pratimā) of the lay follower: right faith, vows, equanimity, fasting on holy days (pauṣadha), standing meditation at night, chastity, renouncing living (uncooked) food, not initiating harmful undertakings, not having them done by servants, refusing food prepared for oneself, and living like a monk (śramaṇa-bhūta).
notes: Order and names follow the Śvetāmbara list (moderate confidence).

paraphrase: The nine kinds of nidāna: a monk or nun who wishes that his austerities should bring him a particular reward — to be reborn as a king, a man, a woman, a god, or even a pious layman — binds himself by that wish and does not reach liberation in that life.
notes: The chapter's stories are set in Mahāvīra's assembly; list of nine recalled with low confidence.

paraphrase: Describes the formation of the body in the womb month by month, the ten decades of a hundred-year life from childhood to decrepitude, the impure contents of the body, and the vast quantity of rice eaten in a lifetime, urging the reader to use the rare human birth for dharma.

Forty-five seers — including Nārada, Asita Devala, Aṅgiras, Yājñavalkya, the Buddhist Vajjiyaputta, Mahākāśyapa and Śāriputra, Maṅkhali Gośāla, Pārśva and Vardhamāna — are each called 'arhat-ṛṣi' and give a short teaching on karma, passion, detachment and the path.
notes: Striking for honouring non-Jain seers as enlightened; list of names moderate confidence.

paraphrase: The Arhat speaks the meaning; the gaṇadharas skilfully compose the sūtras, for the benefit of the teaching; thus scripture proceeds.
notes: 'atthaṃ bhāsai arahā, suttaṃ gaṃthaṃti gaṇaharā niuṇaṃ…'; the verse number differs between editions (low confidence on 92).

paraphrase: In a former birth as Marīci, grandson of Ṛṣabha, the future Mahāvīra left the hard discipline and became a tridaṇḍin ascetic; on hearing that he would be the last Tīrthaṅkara, a vāsudeva and a cakravartin, he danced with pride in his lineage, binding the karma of low status that later caused him to be conceived in a brāhmaṇa womb.
notes: Section-level ref; the story is retold in Hemacandra's Triṣaṣṭi 1 and 10.

paraphrase: The debates of the gaṇadharas: eleven learned brāhmaṇas came to defeat Mahāvīra, each secretly doubting one thing — the soul, karma, the soul's difference from the body, the reality of the elements, rebirth in like form, bondage and liberation, gods, hell-beings, merit and demerit, the other world, and nirvāṇa. Mahāvīra named each one's doubt and resolved it, often by showing that the Vedic sentence behind it (such as 'vijñānaghana evaitebhyo bhūtebhyaḥ samutthāya') had been misread; each became his disciple.
speaker: Mahāvīra
notes: Section spans c. gāthās 1549–2024 (low confidence on the range); the Vedic sentence is from Bṛhadāraṇyaka 2.4.12.

paraphrase: The eighth schism, the Boṭika: at Rathavīrapura, 609 years after the nirvāṇa, Śivabhūti, angered when his teacher Āryakṛṣṇa cut up the precious blanket a king had given him, heard the teacher describe the naked Jinakalpa practice, declared that this alone was true renunciation and went naked; his sister Uttarā followed, but a courtesan covered her, and he taught that women cannot be without clothes and therefore cannot be liberated. So began the Boṭikas.
notes: The Śvetāmbara account of Digambara origins (the Digambaras' view reported by their opponents); section-level ref, details moderate confidence.

paraphrase: During a twelve-year famine the monks scattered and the scripture began to be forgotten; afterwards the saṅgha assembled at Pāṭaliputra and put together the eleven Aṅgas, but no one knew the Dṛṣṭivāda except Bhadrabāhu, then in Nepal practising the 'great breath' meditation. Sthūlabhadra went to learn the Pūrvas from him; after Sthūlabhadra displayed his power by taking the form of a lion before his sisters, Bhadrabāhu refused to teach him the meaning of the last four Pūrvas, giving only the text, so that their meaning was lost.
notes: Canto 9; the mahāprāṇa meditation is named but not described (no practice detail).

paraphrase: The story of Cāṇakya, a Jain layman's son, who raised Candragupta to the throne of Pāṭaliputra and overthrew the Nandas; Candragupta later became a Jain, and Cāṇakya ended his life in a fast.
notes: Canto 8; moderate confidence on the end of the narrative.

paraphrase: The first book tells the twelve previous births of Ṛṣabha — from the caravan-leader Dhana, who first gained right faith by giving alms to monks, to his last birth — and his life as first king and first Tīrthaṅkara, with Bharata's conquests and Bāhubali's renunciation.
notes: Book-level ref.

paraphrase: The tenth book, the life of Mahāvīra: his twenty-seven previous births (from the village headman Nayasāra, through Marīci, to the god in the Puṣpottara palace), his birth, austerities, hardships, omniscience, preaching, the gaṇadharas, the conflict with Gośāla, and his nirvāṇa, with a prophecy of the future.
notes: Book-level ref.

paraphrase: King Śreṇika, doubting the popular Rāmāyaṇa — how could the mighty rākṣasas be defeated by monkeys, how could Kumbhakarṇa sleep six months, how could Rāvaṇa, a learned man, eat flesh? — asks Gautama for the true story; Gautama tells it: the 'monkeys' and 'demons' are human vidyādhara clans, and the other versions are false.
notes: The frame of the Jain Rāma narratives; chapter numbering low confidence.
